title: 2 Samuel
subtitle: David's kingdom and David's house
lead: 2 Samuel is the story of David's reign. It opens with David weeping over Saul and Jonathan, and it closes with an old king buying a threshing floor where the temple will one day stand. Between them David becomes king of Judah at Hebron, then of all Israel, takes Jerusalem, brings the ark of God into it, and hears God promise him a house, a dynasty, that will last forever.

Then the story turns. David takes Bathsheba and has her husband killed, and the prophet Nathan tells him that the sword will never leave his house. Rape, murder, a son's revolt and civil war follow. The book does not hide its hero's sins, and it does not let go of God's promise. Jews and Christians have read that promise (chapter 7) as the root of the hope for a Messiah, a son of David.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): the prophets Gad and Nathan finished the book of Samuel after Samuel's death. Most critical scholars: part of the Deuteronomistic History, edited in the 7th–6th centuries BC from older sources such as a history of David's rise and a court history.
Set about 1010–970 BC, the forty years of David's reign. Some sources may come from David's or Solomon's court; the book reached its present form in the late monarchy or the exile.
Hebron and Jerusalem; the hill country of Judah and Benjamin; Gilead and Mahanaim east of the Jordan; and David's wars with the Philistines, Moab, Aram, Edom and Ammon.
Historical narrative with laments and songs (1:19–27; 3:33–34; 22; 23:1–7), lists of officials and warriors, and a prophetic oracle (chapter 7).
Hebrew. The Hebrew text of Samuel is unusually damaged; the Greek Septuagint and the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a often preserve a better text.

24 chapters, 695 verses. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book in Hebrew; the Greek calls this book 2 Kingdoms (2 Reigns), and the Vulgate and the King James Version subtitle it "the Second Book of the Kings."

audience.to: Israelites who lived after David's forty-year reign and knew his dynasty. The book writes as one looking back: it quotes the old Book of Jashar (1:18) and notes places and customs that last "to this day" (4:3; 6:8; 18:18). As with 1 Samuel, who those readers were depends on the view of how the book was made. They may have been Solomon's court and the tribes of Israel, who wondered whether David's house had any right to rule. They may have been Judah under its later kings. Or they may have been Judeans after 586 BC, with no son of David on the throne.
audience.why: To show how David became king of all Israel, how God promised him a lasting house (7:11–16), and what happened when the king himself broke God's law. The book does not hide David's sins: adultery with Bathsheba, the murder of Uriah, a family torn by rape, murder and revolt. It shows God keeping his promise anyway, through judgment and forgiveness. Knowing the readers changes the reading. Under Solomon, it answers the question of why he, and not an older brother, sat on the throne. Under later kings, it holds them to the standard Nathan held David to. For exiles, it asks whether God's promise to David still stood when there was no king at all. It also gives them a pattern of repentance in David's "I have sinned against the LORD" (12:13).
views: Written by the prophets Gad and Nathan

Jewish tradition says Gad and Nathan finished the book of Samuel after Samuel's death (Bavli Bava Batra 15a; compare 1 Chronicles 29:29). On this view the first readers were Israel in David's and Solomon's days, and the book is a prophetic record that judges the king by God's word.
A court history for Solomon's reign

Leonhard Rost argued that chapters 9–20, with 1 Kings 1–2, form a Succession Narrative: a story of who would succeed David on the throne. He thought someone close to the court wrote it to explain how Solomon came to rule. Gerhard von Rad praised it as the beginning of real history writing. R. N. Whybray read it as political writing in support of Solomon's rule.
A royal apology, or a critique

P. Kyle McCarter and Baruch Halpern read much of the book as a royal apology, that is, a work written to defend a king against charges. On this view it answers those who said David killed Abner, Ish-bosheth and Saul's sons to clear his way. Others, such as Leonhard Delekat and Ernst Würthwein, read the Court History as critical of David and Solomon, written by people who had suffered under the crown.
The Deuteronomistic History, for Josiah's Judah and after the fall

The Deuteronomistic History is the long history from Deuteronomy to Kings, written in the language of Deuteronomy. Martin Noth argued that one writer composed it after 586 BC, probably in Judah, to show why the disaster was just. Noth saw no promise of a future in it. Frank Moore Cross saw an earlier edition under Josiah that put its hope in the promise to David. Gerhard von Rad also found hope in the history. For readers like these, Nathan's oracle (7:12–16) and David's repentance said that God had not finished with David's line.

A few scholars date the David stories much later. John Van Seters thought the Court History was written after the exile, partly to criticize hopes for David's line. A. Graeme Auld argued that Samuel–Kings and Chronicles both grew out of one older shared story of the kings.
Literary readers such as Robert Alter, Meir Sternberg and J. P. Fokkelman leave the date open and read the book as narrative art that shows the cost of power inside a family.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: David reigned about 1010–970 BC, and the book records his reign faithfully, flaws and all, from prophetic and court sources (1 Chronicles 29:29). The Tel Dan stele's 'house of David' shows that a dynasty bore his name.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most academic scholars see a 'Succession Narrative' or 'Court History' (chapters 9–20 with 1 Kings 1–2) and an appendix (21–24) joined into the Deuteronomistic History. Some read the David story as royal apology for a usurper (McCarter, Halpern); minimalists doubt that David ruled a kingdom of any size.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Readers of every school admire the book as narrative art: the sin with Bathsheba turns the story, Nathan's parable traps the king, and the sword never leaves David's house. The narrator rarely says what anyone feels.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis weigh David closely: 'Whoever says David sinned is mistaken' (Shabbat 56a) stands beside his own confession, and God's promise of a lasting house (chapter 7) grounds the hope for a Messiah, son of David.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: The New Testament reads the promise to David (7:12–16) as fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30; Hebrews 1:5), and David's repentance as a pattern of forgiveness (Psalm 51).

authorship: The Talmud says that Samuel wrote the book that bears his name and that Gad the seer and Nathan the prophet finished it (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), since Samuel died before the events of 2 Samuel (1 Samuel 25:1). 1 Chronicles 29:29 names the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the visionary as sources for David's reign. Both prophets appear in 2 Samuel (7; 12; 24:11–19). Notes such as "to this day" (4:3; 6:8) and the citation of the Book of Jashar (1:18) show a writer using older records.
Critical scholarship: older narratives in a larger history

Most critical scholars place 2 Samuel within the Deuteronomistic History (Deuteronomy to Kings), edited in the late monarchy or the exile. Inside it they see older blocks: the end of the History of David's Rise (chapters 1–5), the close of the ark story (6), Nathan's oracle (7), and Leonhard Rost's Succession Narrative or Court History (9–20 with 1 Kings 1–2), admired for its realism and often dated close to Solomon's reign. Chapters 21–24 are an appendix of lists, songs and stories arranged in a ring. Many scholars, such as P. Kyle McCarter and Baruch Halpern, read much of the material as royal apology defending David; others see the Court History as critical of him.

Robert Alter, J. P. Fokkelman, Meir Sternberg and Robert Polzin read 2 Samuel as a carefully built whole: a rise (1–10), a fall that begins with Bathsheba (11–12), and its consequences in David's family (13–20), told by a narrator who shows actions and leaves motives open.

sections.b:
The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Key terms match the rest of the site: YHWH is "the LORD" and Adonai YHWH "Lord GOD" (7:18); YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies" (5:10); hesed is "loyal love" (2:5; 9:1); nagid is "ruler" and melekh "king" (5:2); meshiach YHWH is "the LORD's anointed" (1:14); chozeh is "visionary" (24:11); and tsara'at is "skin disease" (3:29). David's laments (1:19–27; 3:33–34) and his songs (22; 23:1–7) are set in poetic lines.

The Hebrew, the Greek and the Dead Sea scrolls

The Hebrew text of Samuel was damaged in copying more than almost any other book. The Greek Septuagint was translated from a Hebrew text that was often better, and the Dead Sea scroll 4QSam-a (about 50–25 BC) frequently agrees with it, or with the parallel accounts in Chronicles. Where the evidence is strong, the Plain follows the Greek or the scroll and says so in the variant: for example the sleeping doorkeeper (4:6), the ark brought from Baalah (6:2), "with all their strength and with songs" (6:5), and the thousand chariots (8:4). Elsewhere it keeps the Hebrew and shows the other readings beside it: for example the Greek call to set up a pillar for the dead (1:19), the Greek text without "The Bow" (1:18), and the different reasons given for Uzzah's death (6:7), where the Plain keeps the Hebrew. Which Greek matters too. In chapters 1–10 the main Greek manuscript, Codex Vaticanus, is a good witness to the original Greek translation; from 11:2 to the end of the book its text was revised toward the Hebrew (the "kaige" revision), so there the Lucianic manuscripts often carry more weight.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book has three movements. Chapters 1–10 tell David's rise to full power: king of Judah at Hebron, king of all Israel, conqueror of Jerusalem, bearer of the ark, receiver of God's promise, victor on every side. Chapters 11–20 turn on one sin: David takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed, and Nathan tells him the sword will never leave his house (12:10). Rape, murder, exile and civil war follow in his own family. Chapters 21–24 are an appendix, arranged in a ring: a famine and a plague (21; 24), lists of warriors (21:15–22; 23:8–39), and at the center two poems, David's song of deliverance and his last words (22; 23:1–7). The book ends at the threshing floor where the temple will stand.

Chapter 7 is the hinge of the book and one of the most important passages in the Bible. David wants to build God a house; God promises instead to build David a house, a dynasty, and to be a father to David's son: "I will be a father to him, and he will be a son to me" (7:14). His loyal love will never be taken away as it was from Saul. The rest of 2 Samuel tests that promise against David's sins, and the rest of the Bible returns to it again and again: in the psalms (Psalm 89; Psalm 132), in the prophets' hope for a coming son of David (Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Ezekiel 34:23–24), and in the New Testament's proclamation of Jesus (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30; Hebrews 1:5).

The Tel Dan inscription (9th century BC) speaks of the "house of David," showing that a dynasty in Judah traced itself to a founder of that name. Excavations in the City of David have found massive stone structures that some archaeologists date to David's time and others to earlier or later periods, and historians disagree about the size of 10th-century Jerusalem. Traditional readers take 2 Samuel as reliable history, written close to the events by prophets and court writers. Many critical scholars accept that it preserves real memories of an early king but think its picture of an empire from Egypt's border to the Euphrates is enlarged. Minimalist scholars doubt much of it. Few historians now deny that David existed.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read 2 Samuel
sections.b: In Jewish tradition 2 Samuel belongs to the Former Prophets. David is the ideal king and the ancestor of the Messiah, and his repentance after Nathan's rebuke is a model of teshuvah, turning back to God (12:13; Psalm 51). The rabbis also weighed his sins closely: "Whoever says David sinned is mistaken" (Bavli Shabbat 56a) stands beside other voices that hold him fully responsible. Christians read God's promise in chapter 7 as fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, and see in David's grief, repentance and restoration a pattern of grace. Both traditions have read the book as a mirror for rulers: power is a trust from God, and no king is above his law.

spec.title: Claude's theory: a book about houses
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: 2 Samuel is built around the word bayit, "house." It opens with a war between the house of Saul and the house of David (3:1). David builds himself a house of cedar (5:11) and wants to build God a house (7:2), and God promises instead to make David a house (7:11). Then, from the roof of that same house, David sees Bathsheba (11:2) and sends Uriah home "to his house" (11:8), and Nathan says the sword will never leave David's house (12:10). Absalom takes over David's house and lies with his concubines on its roof (16:21–22). The book ends with David buying the site of God's future house (24:18–25). I suggest that the book asks which house will last, the one David builds or the one God builds, and answers that only God's promise holds David's house together. Scholars have often noted the "house" wordplay in chapter 7; reading the whole book through it is my own proposal.

prompts: David's lament on the hills of Gilboa (1:17–27)

A young bearded king, David, sits on a rocky slope at dusk with his head bowed and his robe torn, holding a small lyre loosely in his lap. Before him on a flat stone lie a broken bow and a dented round shield. Behind, the bare dark ridges of Mount Gilboa with no grass, and a few soldiers standing in mourning with dust on their heads.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, simple register lines like an ancient Near Eastern frieze, and a few bold flat shapes of deep blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

A joyful procession climbs a stone road into a hill town. Men carry a gold-covered chest with two winged cherubim on its lid on poles across their shoulders. In front, a bearded king in a short white linen apron whirls with arms raised. Musicians play lyres, hand drums, rattles and a ram's horn. High above in a window of a stone house, a woman in fine clothes, Michal, looks down with a cold face.

reading: P. Kyle McCarter Jr., II Samuel (Anchor Bible, 1984)
The standard critical commentary, especially strong on the Hebrew, Greek and Qumran texts and on David as a historical figure.
A literary translation of 1 and 2 Samuel with notes on the book's narrative art.
A. A. Anderson, 2 Samuel (Word Biblical Commentary, 1989)
A thorough commentary on text, history and interpretation.
David Toshio Tsumura, The Second Book of Samuel (NICOT, 2019)
A careful evangelical commentary that reads the Masoretic Text closely and the book as a literary whole.
A theological commentary alert to power, politics and the human David.
A historian's reading of David as a ruthless politician, and of the book as royal apology.
